skill_side_findings.contradiction_1_support_test_condition_2: The three-condition test makes a cluster article that merely forgot to link back a 'collision finding' that gets no link, while linking-templates.md requires every pillar<->cluster gap to get a row. What you do have is the statement in your own export: "we think of /blog/bike-maintenance-guide as the pillar"... ambiguous_expectations_eval_improvement.issue: The clause that failed bundles a SEQUENCING test with an implicit SCOPE requirement, and the prompt pulls the other way. Eval 4's prompt asks to 'optimize anchor text across the site' and then 'wrap it all into the full implementation plan with phases'; the expectation requires the orphan to be FIXED and fixed first. A deliverable that reads the brief as anchor-only, declares the orphan out of scope, and says so four times fails an expectation it never saw. Two honest readings exist. Suggested split: e4.4a - the plan carries the Step 7 shape and fixture-baselineable tracking; e4.4b - structural fixes (the orphan's inbound links and the 404 repoint) appear in the critical-fix phase ahead of anchor rewording, and a plan that declines to add links fails this whether or not it says so. Whichever the coordinator rules, the expectation should say it, because today it reads as sequencing and grades as scope.

Both contain a raw `~~` category token in their own prose ('requiring ~~search console / rank tracking data', 'the ~~web crawler connector route'). Legitimate on an operator surface, and this run resolved every token correctly - but the suite has no expectation forbidding a token in the DELIVERABLE (coverage gap C6), so the only place `~~` appears in the instrument is where it could be misread as licence. Worth a one-line addition to the fabrication expectations: 'no `~~category` token appears on a client-read surface; a labelled operator block is not one.'

The lead clause is general ('the anchor audit works the planted problems with fixture-true counts and named populations') and the body is a closed list of three specific tests. Defect D1 - a wrong anchor count in the audit's own prose - satisfies every listed test and breaches the lead clause. This grader graded on the list and reported D1 separately, and says so, but two graders could rule differently on the same sentence. Either scope the lead clause to the enumerated items, or add 'and no count stated anywhere in the anchor section contradicts the audit's own tables'.

Not an expectation defect but the rubric behind one. A link can be in two grade classes at once - the two 'read our guide' instances are both content-free (❌ 0) and the same anchor on two targets (⚠️ 0.5) - and the rubric does not say which wins. §7's worked example takes ⚠️; both deliverables take ❌ and argue for it. The displayed score is 7 either way here, which is luck. One sentence in §3 ('where a link falls in two classes, the lower grade applies') would make the Anchor Score reproducible between two graders, which is what §1 says it is for.
